messages.subject: new contributor & von mises distribution
parts:
See comments below on Daniel Mitchell contributing
code for some circular distributions.

On 9/27/12 2:39 PM, Daniel Mitchell wrote:
> Thanks for your comments Bob, they clarified some things for me.
>
> It's no trouble to add the Bessel functions.
>
> I've attached my latest code. I think it's getting close to a working state.

It looks good. I've reattached so everyone else can
check it out.

It was already pretty close last time. I'll attach
some code comments below after the admin details on merging.

> A word on how I'm working: I cloned the stan repository locally and
> created a circular-distributions branch. I would like to contribute
> von mises, wrapped normal, and wrapped cauchy distributions, as well
> as the bessel functions you asked for. I don't mind emailing you
> patches, but maybe it would be easier if I could share this branch
> with you. What's the preferred method for doing so? Should I just
> 'Create a clone' on code.google.com?

I'm not the git expert here (Ben is). What do you mean
by a clone on code.google.com? You shouldn't start
another project, and your own clone of our repository
would be local to you, right

We could give you permissions to push to Stan's
repository on Google Code, and then your branch is
something we'd have easy access to for merging.
I'm about to head out town for the weekend, so how
about setting this up after the 1.0.2 release
which will be tomorrow or Monday? That'll get in
Daniel Lee's patches to the auto-diff vectorization
expression templates.

I believe you can also create a diff file that we
can just apply. Ben's sent them to me before, but
I don't know how to create them.

I believe you can also send us a pull request from
your own clone of the repository.

Any suggestions, Ben?

CODE COMMENTS

Could I ask that you try to keep the lines shorter? Ideally
80 chars or less. And stylistically, can you not start
lines with "{"? I'd rather see this:

template<bool propto, typename T_y, typename T_loc, typename T_scale>
inline typename return_type<T_y,t_loc,T_scale>::type
von_mises_log(T_y const& y, T_loc const& mu, T_scale const& kappa)
{ return von_mises_log<propto>(y, mu, kappa, stan::math::default_policy()); }

rewritten as:

template<bool propto, typename T_y, typename T_loc, typename T_scale>
inline typename return_type<T_y,t_loc,T_scale>::type
von_mises_log(T_y const& y, T_loc const& mu, T_scale const& kappa) {
return von_mises_log<propto>(y, mu, kappa, stan::math::default_policy());
}

Having now griped about style, we're really not that picky about it.
Just please don't write "if(...)" or "for(...)" without a space
or "fun (...)" with a space. (Just my own peeve!)

Daniel Lee's working on refactoring the vectorizations, though,
so our code base has drifted a bit. Nothing that should
be hard to update against -- same abstractions with slightly
different implementations.

You don't need the length check -- the check_consistent_sizes
will take care of it for you, and if it doesn't, it should
be fixed so it does. All the vectors need to have the same
length. Arguably, if that length is zero, the functions should
just return log prob = 0.

Is the variate y here constrained to (0,2*pi)? If so, there
should be a check.

The code looks good. You can save some time by making
the evaluations of the heavy functions conditional.
For instance, where you have:

// Reusable values. These computations should be moved outside the loop if possible.
double const kappa_sin_mu_minus_y = kappa_dbl * std::sin(mu_dbl - y_dbl);
...

// Gradients.
if (!is_constant<typename is_vector<T_y>::type>::value)
operands_and_partials.d_x1[n] += kappa_sin_mu_minus_y;
if (!is_constant<typename is_vector<T_loc>::type>::value)
operands_and_partials.d_x2[n] -= kappa_sin_mu_minus_y;

you almost certainly want to do this instead:

double kappa_sin_mu_minus_y;
if (!constant T_y || !constant T_loc)
kappa_sin_mu_minus_y = kappa_dbl * std::sin(mu_dbl - y_dbl);

and so on.

Also, we only want to compute values once if we can in the
vectorization. The existing normal.hpp isn't a good example as
it didn't apply this optimization, either. The new normal.hpp
should be better.

Having said that, we're happy to put in things that work and
improve their speed later.

To that end, we really need the unit tests! You can either write
them directly or try to get your head around Daniel Lee's
distribution testing framework. I'm sure he can help.

We should probably pull that pesky log(2 * pi) up into a constant
in stan/math/constants.hpp. We can do this kind of cleanup later.
We haven't been real good about it in our own distributions. It's
actually faster to have constants outside classes because then
you don't have to check if they've been instantiated when using
them.

- Bob

On Thursday, September 27, 2012 4:23:48 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> A word on how I'm working: I cloned the stan repository locally and
> created a circular-distributions branch. I would like to contribute
> von mises, wrapped normal, and wrapped cauchy distributions, as well
> as the bessel functions you asked for. I don't mind emailing you
> patches, but maybe it would be easier if I could share this branch
> with you. What's the preferred method for doing so?  Should I just
> 'Create a clone' on code.google.com?

I'm not the git expert here (Ben is).  What do you mean
by a clone on code.google.com?  You shouldn't start
another project, and your own clone of our repository
would be local to you, right

That is more a GitHub thing (which we have talked about moving to someday). I think "git format-patch" or "git send-email" would be best, but in this case, that pretty much amounts to sending the new .hpp files for each circular distribution to Bob, which you already did. Bob can save them locally, git add, and push. The only disadvantage of the latter is that it looks like Bob did all the work in git log and so forth.

I believe you can also create a diff file that we
can just apply.  Ben's sent them to me before, but
I don't know how to create them.

Probably with git format-patch. But simply doing "git diff -p master > /tmp/mypatch.patch" often works if either you haven't pulled from origin/master into master since you branched or if you have pulled from origin/master into both local master and the local branch (so all the stuff Bob / Daniel have done in the last few days isn't duplicated in the patch.

Ben

P.S. We should write down an outside contributor HOWTO.
